turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's books people can read on this-
turns.zh: 所以有书可以读——

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Right. Ours came before, but that's okay.
turns.zh: 对。我们的比它早，但没关系。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. Okay. Good to know.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。好。知道了。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: I will say anything that spreads the word and anything that helps people learn how to engage with each other in ways that build relationship, I'm all for.
turns.zh: 我会说，任何传播这个、任何帮人学会怎么以建立关系的方式互动的东西，我都全力支持。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that attitude. Okay, so the structure again is just when you do some behavior, I feel an emotion. By the way, is there a flyer or handout? I think the book has these of just emotions. Okay, cool. And feelings.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个态度。好，所以结构再说是：当你做了某个行为，我感受到一种情绪。顺便，有传单或讲义吗？我想书里有这些情绪、感受的东西。好，酷。还有感受。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: The vocabulary of feelings is an appendix in the book.
turns.zh: 感受词汇表在书的附录里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, great.
turns.zh: 好，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: As is the formula.
turns.zh: 公式也是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, great. So by the book, if you want to get really good at this stuff, is there anything online we can point people to, or?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好，太棒了。所以按书来，如果你想真把这事儿练好，有什么线上东西能指给人们吗？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: We got a picture of the... I'll send you a couple of slides.
turns.zh: 我们有张……图，我发你几页 slide。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: And then you can just say, here are the slides.
turns.zh: 然后你就可以说，这是那些 slide。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. So we'll link to that in the show notes. And as you talk through all of these lessons and pieces of advice, it makes so much sense why this is something you need to do. Because I imagine what's happening in the class here is you do this with someone and then you hear the reality and it often surprises you. Right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以我们会在 show notes 里链过去。当你过这些教训和建议时，你完全能理解为什么这是必须做的事。因为我想象课上发生的是：你和某人做这个，然后你听到那个现实，它常常让你惊讶。对吧？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Exactly. Because often we say it takes two to know one, I don't know what impact I'm having on you until you tell me. And I have to be willing to be a little vulnerable to ask. And if we go back to that first activity that you asked me to describe way at the beginning, then we put them back in pairs and we say, okay, now that you've learned a little bit about feedback, tell your partner what they did that made it easier for you to disclose more and be more willing to be more vulnerable and/or what they did that made it a little harder. And right there in the moment, you learned something about yourself that you might never have known. Somebody says, you looked away as I was talking, you might not have even known you did that. You looked at your watch. And I love this. (00:52:34): One of my greatest moments when I was teaching was that I asked a question. I was teaching in a big lecture hall at the law school, and they didn't have any clocks on the wall. And I asked a question and a student began answering, and I just glanced at my watch just because I was trying to figure out where I was in terms of when I had to wrap up. And he walked up to me after class and he said, "Professor, I felt disrespected when you looked at your watch while I was answering," I hugged him. Well, first I asked him if it was okay, "Is it okay if I hug you?" And then I hugged him.
turns.zh: 完全对。因为我们常说“认识一个自己需要两个人”——我不告诉你，我永远不知道我对你有什么影响。而我得愿意稍稍脆弱才能去问。回到你最开始让我描述的第一個活动：我们把他们重新成对，说，好，现在你学了一点反馈，告诉你搭档：他们做了什么让你更容易披露更多、更愿意更脆弱；和/或他们做了什么让它更难一点。就在那一刻，你学到关于自己可能从不知道的东西。有人会说：你说话时看向别处，你可能根本不知道你这么做了。你看了手表。我就爱这个。（00:52:34）我教书时最棒的时刻之一是：我问了个问题。我在法学院的大讲堂教课，墙上没钟。我问了个问题，一个学生开始回答，我只是瞥了眼手表，因为我想搞清楚离该收尾还有多久。下课后他走过来对我说：“教授，你在我回答时看手表，我觉得不被尊重。”我抱了他。嗯，我先问“我可以抱你吗？”然后抱了他。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I love how so much of this is like, we never get this feedback in real life. No one ever tells us this thing you did is distracting them, annoying them, making them feel like they're not being heard.
turns.zh: 而且我就爱这一点：我们在真实生活里从没得到这种反馈。从没人告诉我们，你做的这件事在分散他们注意力、烦他们、让他们觉得没被听见。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: And then guess what? Then he leaves and then somebody says, how was that? He says, oh, she's really disrespectful. And then pretty soon nobody's ever even been there. But my reputation is that I don't respect students. That's how stuff gets out of control.
turns.zh: 然后猜怎么着？他走了，然后有人说“怎么样？”他说“哦，她真不尊重人”。然后很快没人真正在场过。但我的名声变成“我不尊重学生”。事情就是这么失控的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And you wish people would tell you, right? Everybody wants this, but it's so hard and uncomfortable to tell anyone negative feedback.
turns.zh: 对。你希望人们告诉你，对吧？每个人都想要这个，但告诉别人负面反馈太难、太不舒服了。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Which by the way, I never used the word negative when it comes to feedback.
turns.zh: 顺便，说到反馈，我从不说“负面”这个词。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Okay.
turns.zh: 好。好。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: So feedback is either constructive or complimentary. Constructive feedback is there's something you're doing that is problematic, and the purpose of it is let's move to a problem solving conversation like with Andy and me. The purpose of complimentary feedback is, wow, that's the third time you've handed in that report early and completely, and you even went above and beyond and did this and this. I can't tell you how much I appreciate that, how lucky I feel that you work for me. And if I'm telling you this, because if there's ever something that you want that we're not giving you, I want to make sure you know that I want to talk about it. By the way, same formula. Now compare that to nice job, thanks, right? All feedback is data. So all feedback is positive. More data is always better than less data.
turns.zh: 所以反馈要么是建设性的，要么是赞美的。建设性反馈是：你在做某件有问题的事，它的目的是开启一个解决问题的对话，像 Andy 和我那样。赞美性反馈的目的是：哇，这是你第三次提前且完整地交那份报告，你甚至超出预期做了这个那个。我无法告诉你我多感激、你为我工作我感到多幸运。如果我告诉你这个，是因为如果将来有什么你想要的、我们没给的，我想确保你知道我想聊这个。顺便，同样的公式。现在对比“干得好，谢了”，对吧？所有反馈都是数据。所以所有反馈都是正面的。更多数据总比更少数据好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I agree. That's a great lesson there. To maybe make this even more practical for listeners that are maybe working on a product and say they have to give feedback in a product design or to a colleague who did something wrong. Is there an example that you could share of just in the workplace.
turns.zh: 我同意。那是很好的教训。为了让听众更实用——比如在做产品、要在产品设计上给反馈，或给犯了错的同事反馈——能在职场里分享个例子吗？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: I'm glad you asked that, because first of all, we're not talking about performance feedback and we're not necessarily talking about feedback on a task. What we're talking about is interpersonal feedback. And the reason it's so important is that if you don't take care of that, then that other feedback becomes unresolved. When you leave the interpersonal stuff unresolved, then the other feedback doesn't go well because the real problem is that I'm still pissed off that you never answered my phone call. So now I'm going to make it all about how this feature really is never going to work. Here's an example. Somebody walks into... A manager or a team leader or whatever, walks into a room meeting, starts a meeting by say, so I want to make sure we hear from everybody. I want to make sure that we have a very full conversation. (00:55:58): I want to talk about X. And now let's say that I start to say something and before I have finished, he says, yeah, and the other thing we should talk about is blah, blah. And then a little later a similar thing happens. I start to suggest that there's another way to look at this and he turns back to somebody else, what somebody else had said and never says anything in response to what I just said. And I'm being very specific here, very behaviorally specific. And then after a while, what happens to me is I feel less and less inclined to offer up anything. Now, maybe he doesn't care, but if he cares because he started by think he wanted to hear from everybody, then I'm not being very caring if I don't tell him what the impact was of his behavior. So I don't call him out in the middle of the meeting because I don't want to embarrass him, but I might go to his office later and say, "So, John, do you have a few minutes?" I have an observation. (00:57:07): I've got something that I experienced that you might want to know. "Sure, Carole." So when I started to say x, you did y. When I started to say z, you did it. I said, and when that you started the meeting by saying you want to hear from everybody. When that happened, I felt less and less... I felt shut down, and I felt less and less inclined to offer up my opinion. Maybe that's okay, but I wondered whether you knew that that was the impact. And I'm telling you, because as far as I am concerned, in that meeting, you did not accomplish your stated desire. Your desired outcome was to hear from everybody. And after a while, I just gave up trying to give you my...
turns.zh: 我很高兴你问，因为首先，我们谈的不是绩效反馈，也不一定是任务反馈。我们谈的是人际反馈。它之所以重要，是因为如果你不处理那个，别的反馈就悬而未决。当你把人际的事留着不解决，别的反馈就进行不好，因为真正的问题是：我还对你从没回我电话耿耿于怀。所以我现在要把它全变成“这功能真的永远行不通”。举个例子。某人走进……一个经理或团队 leader 什么的，走进会议室，开会开头说：我想确保我们听到每个人的声音。我想确保我们有非常充分的对话。（00:55:58）我想聊 X。然后假设我开始说点什么，还没说完，他说：对，另一件该聊的是 blah blah。然后一会儿又类似发生。我开始建议有另一种看这事的方式，他转回别人、对别人之前说的回应，对我刚说的什么都不回应。我这里说得很具体、行为上很具体。然后过了一会儿，我发生的是：我越来越不想贡献任何东西。现在，也许他不在乎，但如果他在乎——因为他开头说想听每个人的——那如果我不告诉他他的行为造成了什么影响，我就不够 caring。所以我不会在会议中途点他名，因为不想让他尴尬，但我可能晚点去他办公室说：“John，有几分钟吗？我有个观察。”（00:57:07）我有个我经历的事你可能想知道。“当然，Carole。”所以当我开始说 x，你做了 y。当我开始说 z，你做了。我说，当 t……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, it's like you need to solve these pinches as you described early, because all of this comes back to these are relationships, they matter because that's the way we get everything done. And if you just ignore these things, your relationship's going to be hurt. You're not going to be able to accomplish the things you want to accomplish. It's almost like something you need to do even though it feels hard.
turns.zh: 嗯，就像你说的，要在它还小（pinch）时解决，因为这一切都回到：这些是关系，它们重要，因为那是我们把事做成的方式。如果你忽略这些，关系会受伤。你没法完成你想完成的事。这几乎是件你必须做的事，尽管感觉难。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Absolutely. And that's why I say that feedback builds relationships because by the way, if I'm doing something that I'm, I wish I hadn't done, it's not that I'm going to be like, "Oh yeah, I'm so glad I did that." But if I recognize that it would've been easier for you not to say anything because it would've been more comfortable, but because you cared about me, you actually said something to me, that talk about something that builds relationship.
turns.zh: 绝对。这就是为什么我说反馈建立关系——因为顺便，如果我在做一件我希望自己没做的事，我不是会说“哦对，我好高兴我做了”。但如果我意识到：你不说会更舒服、更容易，但你因为关心我，真的对我说了——那就正是建立关系的东西。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to the antenna as you described feels like one of the most important skills you teach people is to build this antenna both of yourself, which is you could to think is easier, but maybe often not, but also understanding how the other person feels. And you have this concept of the art of inquiry and how powerful that is. Can you just talk about what that is?
turns.zh: 回到你说的天线，它感觉是你教人最重要的技能之一：建立自己的天线——你可能觉得更容易，但也许常常不是——也理解对方感受。你还有“询问的艺术”（art of inquiry）这个概念，以及它多有力。能聊聊那是什么吗？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Oh, yeah. I'm glad you brought that up, because inquiry is a fundamental component of strong interpersonal relationships for a couple of reasons. And first of all, let's stop and note, inquiry comes the root of the word inquiry is quest. Quest means to be in search of and not knowing what you're going to find, not the way most people think about questions and inquiries. Most of the time people ask a question to confirm a hypothesis. "Don't you think you're just trying to discredit John by doing that?" That's not inquiry. "Don't you think you'd just be better off letting that go?" That's not inquiry. And by the way, another thing to note in artful inquiry, first of all, you have to suspend judgment. You cannot be curious if you've already decided you know what's going on someone else. You can always go back to being judgmental, but you got to suspend it long enough to see if there's something for you to learn. (01:00:12): And then the way you ask the question matters, questions that can be answered with yes or no are typically limiting questions and aren't going to be very productive. Questions that start with why, why did you do that? Are going to make me defensive? Or worse, why are you crying? Well, is that going to make me want to tell you more about why I am upset or why are you upset? Right away I'm going to go into, "Oh no, I'm not upset. It's not a big deal." Or I'm going to go into a place that's not necessarily very productive because this reminds me of how my mother always scolded me. Neither one is going to be very productive. So questions that start with what? What's this about? What's going on? Where is this manifesting? When did you see this happen last? How might we go about unpacking what's going on? Where is this happening most? When, where, how, stay away from why. And it's a whole art.
turns.zh: 哦对。我很高兴你提这个，因为询问是强人际关系的基本组成，有几个原因。首先，停下注意：询问（inquiry）这个词根是 quest，quest 是“搜寻”、且不知道会找到什么——不是大多数人想问题、想询问的方式。大多数时候人问问题是为了证实假设。“你不觉得你那么做只是想抹黑 John 吗？”那不是询问。“你不觉得你放手会更好吗？”那不是询问。顺便，在巧妙询问里另一点要注意：首先，你得悬置判断。如果你已经断定你懂别人在发生什么，你不可能好奇。你随时可以回到评判，但你得悬置足够久，看有没有值得你学的。（01:00:12）然后你问问题的方式重要：能用 yes/no 回答的问题通常是限制性问题，不会很有产出。以“为什么”开头的问题——“你为什么那么做？”——会让我防卫。或者更糟，“你为什么哭？”嗯，那会让我想告诉你更多我为什么难过吗，还是“你为什么难过？”我立马会进入“哦不，我没难过，没什么大不了”，或者进入一个不一定有产出的状态，因为这让我想起我妈总怎么骂我。两种都不太有产出。所以用“什么”开头的问题：这是关于什么？在发生什么？这体现在哪？你上次看到这发生是什么时候？我们怎么去拆解在发生什么？哪里发生最多？何时、何地、如何，避开为什么。这是一整套艺术。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else you teach people and you're big on is that people can actually change themselves. I think a lot of people might feel like, I'm just not good at this. I'm not good at giving feedback. I'm not good at maybe asking questions. I'm just like, I don't know. Talk about what you found about the change people see and why it's actually possible and how.
turns.zh: 你教的、也很强调的另一点是：人其实能改变自己。我觉得很多人会觉得“我就是不擅长这个。我不擅长给反馈。我不擅长提问。我就是……不知道”。聊聊你发现的人的改变，以及为什么真的可能、怎么做到？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Well, for starters, to any of your listeners, one of my very favorite authors is Carol Dweck who wrote a book called Mindset and you put a word yet at the end of any of those, I don't know how yet, I'm not like that yet, changes the meaning of the whole thing. And by the way, talk about updating a mental model, instant update of a mental model. And the other thing that I'll say is we are all capable of changing our behavior. We cannot change our personality. We are born wired with personalities. I am very outgoing and extroverted as might come as a shock to all of you. And you know what? When I overdo it, I suck all the oxygen out of the room and one of the behaviors I had to learn, and it takes discipline to engage in was zipping it a little more so that others could speak up more. (01:02:40): And my incentive was that I actually really wanted to learn more about what was going on for them and I wasn't going to learn anything unless I shut up long enough for them to tell me. So behavior is something we all have control over. Now when I give somebody feedback and they tell me, well, I can't do that. If I've asked them to change a behavior, then I'll say, I'm sorry, I don't think I can accept I can't. I will accept I don't want to or I don't have it, but I don't have to accept I can't. So I'd just like you to own the fact that it's a choice that you're making.
turns.zh: 首先，对任何听众：我最爱的作者之一是 Carol Dweck，写了《Mindset》（心态）那本书。你在任何那些话后面加个“yet（还）”——“我还不知道怎么”“我还没那样”——就改变了整句话的意思。顺便，说到更新心智模型，那是个即时更新。另一件我会说的是：我们都有能力改变行为。我们改不了性格。性格是天生的。我非常外向，可能对你们所有人是个惊喜。你知道，当我过度了，我会把房间里的氧气吸光，而我得学的一个行为——需要纪律去做到——是多 zip 一下嘴，让别人多说。（01:02:40）我的动力是：我真的想多了解他们那边在发生什么，而我不闭嘴够久让他们告诉我，我就学不到任何东西。所以行为是我们都能控制的。现在，当我给某人反馈、他们告诉我“嗯，我做不到”。如果我让他们改个行为，我会说：抱歉，我不接受“我做不到”。我会接受“我不想”或“我没有”，但我不必接受“我做不到”。所以我想让你承认：那是你做的一个选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of along those lines, something, I don't know if this is from your book, but I saw somewhere you said that it's possible to say almost anything to almost anyone if you have the necessary skills. How do people build these skills? I know we talked about a lot of this through the structure focusing on your side of the net, but just how do you avoid people getting defensive?
turns.zh: 顺着这个，有句话——不知道是不是你书里的——我在某处看到你说：如果有必要的技能，几乎可以对几乎任何人说几乎任何事。人怎么建这些技能？我知道我们透过“守在你那侧网”的结构聊了很多，但你怎么避免人变得防卫？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: First of all, let's make sure that we point out that what we're doing here is we're shifting probabilities of success, we're not guaranteeing anything. And let's say that you do your best and you stay on your side of the net and you give somebody feedback and they go bonkers and they call you all kinds of names and they write... Now there's an opportunity to learn something else that everybody learns in these programs, which is called repair. How do you repair when something goes sideways? Because no matter how good you are, no matter how skilled you get, no matter what your intent was, sometimes it won't work. And then you've got to know how to repair. And that's why, remember I told you that our facilitators have a unique set of skills? And that's because they have to allow messes to happen otherwise nobody's going to learn how to repair. And repair often goes back to some of what we've already talked about. Let's start with I come in the kitchen, my husband's struggling. I say to him, "Can I help you with that?" He says, "Don't tell me what to do." (01:05:04): I'm sure none of your listeners can relate to this story. And I say, instead of, "I wasn't trying to tell you what to do, I was just trying to be helpful. What a kind of way to respond to my offering help is that?" I say, "What did you hear me say?" One of the most powerful things you can do when somebody responds in a way that feels very unexpected and out of whack with what you just said is go back to, "What did you hear me say?" Because nine times out of 10 what they heard is not what you said. He said, "I heard you say I didn't know what I was doing." Now, by the way, it didn't matter. That's not what I said. And I didn't say, that's not what I said. I said, "Wow, really glad I asked, because now that I understand that that's what you heard, I understand why you reacted the way you did." And I said, "Let me try it again." (01:06:04): One of the ways that I show somebody that I love them is I offer to help and what would you like me to do if in a situation like this when I see you struggling? He says, "Wait for me to ask." And that was 25 years ago, and that has served us very well because we've been married 37 years, 39 years. And if we go back to feedback, you give somebody feedback, they get super defensive. By the way, net jumping invites net jumping, so they're likely to net jump too. And by the way, the minute you label somebody or you're over the net. In fact you sent me something that was really interesting that I wanted to find here because you said "Nobody is born with genes for being rude or self-involved." Well, guess what? (01:06:56): Rude and self-involved are labels that is not behaviorally specific. So calling somebody rude or self-involved is just going to make them defensive. But saying, I was interrupted three times, and I'm telling you this because you said you wanted to hear my opinion and I just thought you should know that I was put off by being interrupted, much less likely to incite defensiveness.
turns.zh: 首先，我们要明确：我们在这里做的是改变成功的概率，不是保证什么。假设你尽力了、守在你那侧网、给某人反馈，然后他们炸了、用各种词骂你、写……现在有机会学别的东西，每个走这些项目的人都学到，叫“修复”（repair）。当事情搞砸了怎么修复？因为不管你多好、多熟练、意图多好，有时就是不行。那你得知道怎么修复。这就是为什么我告诉过你，我们的引导者有套独特技能？因为他们得允许混乱发生，否则没人学怎么修复。而修复常回到我们聊过的某些东西。比如我进厨房，我老公在挣扎。我说：“要我帮忙吗？”他说：“别指挥我。”（01:05:04）我相信你听众没人能对上这个故事。而我没说“我不是想指挥你，我只是想帮忙。你这么回我帮忙也太……”。我说：“你听到我说的什么了？”当某人回得完全出乎意料、和你刚说的对不上时，你能做的最有力的事之一是回到：“你听到我说的什么了？”因为十次有九次，他们听到的不是你说的。他说：“我听到你说我不知道我在干嘛。”顺便，没关系。那不是我说的。我也没说“那不是我说的”。我说：“哇，真高兴我问了，因为现在我明白那是你听到的，我理解你为什么那样反应了。”我说：“让我再试一次。”（01:06:04）我向人展示……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Just hearing what actually happened, staying on your side of the net.
turns.zh: 绝对。只是听到实际发生了什么，守在你那侧网。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So again, this always comes back to I could see this being so effective doing this in a class versus just listening to us and like, okay, I'm going to start staying in my side of the net and I'm going to prepare relationships. Are there any other examples of exercises you do in the class that might be helpful to people just to hear how you learn some of these things?
turns.zh: 所以再说，这总回到：我能想象在课上做这个多有效，对比只是听我们聊——然后“好，我要开始守在我那侧网、我要预备关系”。课上还有别的练习例子，能帮人听听你们怎么学这些吗？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Every chapter in the book has a section at the end called Deepen Your Learning and those deep in your learning sections, every single one of them has a suggested activity, something you can go do, and some of those come from some of the things we do in the classroom. So that's one place to start in terms of trying to find very tactical and practical ways of applying some of this. The other thing that we often do, I often do in leaders in Tech, I used to do this less at Stanford because they did a lot of this in their T groups and they were actually in real time with each other putting everything they were learning to use. But sometimes with my execs in Leaders in Tech, I will, for example, put them in a trio and I will say to you, so Lenny, I want you to think of somebody who you would like to give feedback to and I want you to tell me what's the behavior they're engaging in? (01:09:04): How does it make you feel? What would be behind you wanting to tell them? What would be your desired outcome to the conversation? Then I become you, you become your difficult person because you know them and I don't, and we role play because you've now told me what you need, what you want, what's going on for you, and then you have to play your difficult person as well as you can. The third person's usually the observer who pinch hits and says, "Carole, I think that was over the net." "Carole, I don't think that was a behavior." And by the way, we say, I feel insert feeling, nine times out of 10 people say, I feel that, or I feel like, I feel that you don't care is not a feeling. (01:09:56): I feel like it doesn't matter, is not a feeling. I feel that you're not committed is not a feeling. In fact, they're all over the net. You're almost guaranteed to be over the net when you start I feel and put in like or that, guaranteed. Very easy hack. I feel pull up vocabulary feeling, you can't say grammatically correctly. I feel that sad or I feel that angry, or I feel that irritated or I feel like disappointed, doesn't work.
turns.zh: 书的每一章结尾都有个叫“深化你的学习”的部分，每一个都有个建议活动，你能去做，其中一些来自我们在课堂做的。所以那是个开始、找非常落地实用的方法应用这些的地方。我们常在 Leaders in Tech 做的另一件事——我在斯坦福做得少点，因为他们在 T 组里实时互相把所有学的用上——但我有时和 Leaders in Tech 的高管们，比如把他们分成三人组，我对你说：Lenny，我想让你想一个你想给反馈的人，告诉我他们在做的行为是什么？（01:09:04）那让你什么感受？你为什么想告诉他们？你希望对话达到什么结果？然后我变成你，你变成你那个难搞的人——因为你了解他们、我不了解——我们角色扮演，因为你已经告诉我要什么、想要什么、你这边发生什么，然后你也得尽量演好你的难搞的人。第三个人通常是观察者，随时插话：“Carole，我觉得那过网了。”“Carole，我觉得那不是个行为。”顺便，我们说“我感到+感受”，十次有九次人说“我觉得 that”或“我觉得 like”——“我觉得你不在乎”不是感受。（01:09:56）“我觉得这无所谓”不是感受。“我觉得你没投入”不是感受。事实上，它们都过网了。你以“我感到”开头、加“like”或“that”，基本保证过网。超简单的 hack：我用“我感到”+从感受词汇表拉一个感受，你语法上没法说“我感到 that 难过”“我感到 that 生气”“我感到 that 恼……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is amazing marriage advice going to, I need to remember these things.
turns.zh: 这是太棒的婚姻建议，我得记住这些。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Yeah. Many married couples have bought the book together and read it together actually, which is cool.
turns.zh: 对。很多已婚夫妇一起买了这本书、一起读，挺酷的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a few other things I want to touch on that I love. One is a tip that you share. You call it advise hinders relationships.
turns.zh: 还有几个我想碰的、我喜欢的点。一个是你分享的贴士。你叫它“建议阻碍关系”。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Oh, I'm really glad you asked me about that because two things, a couple of things. First of all, leaders often believe this is another mental model that they have to have all the answers, and that is actually a pretty, it's not a very productive mental model or belief because first of all, puts a huge amount of pressure on the leader. Now suddenly I always have to know and what happens when I don't know. Second of all, I believe a leader's job is to ensure the best answer is found. It doesn't matter whether it comes from me or anywhere else in the organization. It also allows for the possibility that somebody else may have a better answer than me. And a really, really good solution has been squelched and never surfaced because people are afraid to say, well, I see it a little differently. What if we did this? (01:11:50): We had a or disaster as a result of that. The other thing about advice is that it creates even bigger power differentials between people. So if you're the leader or you're in the higher power position to start with, then giving me advice is only going to make me feel even lower power as opposed to, well, let's think about this together. Let's be thought partners. Often when we give advice, it's a good thing to stop yourself and ask yourself, "Who am I doing this for? Am I doing this for me so that I can puff myself up with everything I know or am I doing it for you because this is really going to help you and make you better?" (01:12:34): Nine times out of 10, being a thought partner as you explore the various options and coming to your own solution is both going to help you develop more, and then you're not going to have to come ask me again if the only time you ever learn is when you come ask me and you don't go through any of the work or figuring out how I got to that answer, well, then I've just made more work for myself.
turns.zh: 哦，我真的很高兴你问我这个，因为几件事。首先，领导者常相信——这是另一个心智模型——他们得有所有答案，而那其实是个挺不高效的心智模型或信念，因为首先它给领导者巨大压力。现在我总得知道，而我不知道时怎么办？其次，我相信领导者的工作是确保找到最好的答案。它来自我还是组织别处不重要。它也允许这种可能：别人也许有比我更好的答案。而一个真的很好的方案被压住、从没浮出，因为人们不敢说“嗯，我有点不同看法。如果我们这样做呢？”（01:11:50）我们就因此有过 or 灾难。关于建议的另一件事是：它制造更大的权力差。所以如果你是领导者、或你本来就在更高权力位，给我建议只会让我感觉权力更低——而不是“我们一起想想。我们做思考伙伴”。常当我们给建议，停一下问自己是个好事：“我为谁做这个？是为我——好让我用我知道的一切把自己 puff 起来？还是为你——因为这真能帮你、让你更好？”（01:12:34）十次有九次，做思考伙伴、一起探索各种选项、让你自己得出方案，既帮你怎么发展，而且你不必再来问我——如果你只在来问我时才学、从不用心或搞清我是怎么得到那个答案的，那我只是给自己制造更多工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's this great Harvard Business Review post I just read about monkeys on your back. Have you heard of this?
turns.zh: 我刚读了篇超棒的 HBR 文章，关于“背上的猴子”。你听过吗？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 听过。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Where basically as a manager, people are always trying to put monkeys on your back to have you solve their problem, and your job as a manager is to keep the monkeys on their own backs and help them.
turns.zh: 对。基本就是：作为经理，人们总想把猴子放你背上、让你解决他们的问题，而经理的工作是让猴子留在他们自己背上、帮他们。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Yes, and I'm glad you brought that up because people then have become so used to the quick shortcut is you'll just give me the answer. First of all, you have enabled powerlessness. You certainly haven't helped them learn and grow. If you at all think your job as a manager is to at least sometimes do that, and sometimes people will say, "Can't you just give me the answer?" And then I always just say, I could and here's why I'm not going to because I don't think that'll serve you because that's not my job. My job isn't just to give you the answers. My job is to turn you into somebody who eventually will just know what the right answer is.
turns.zh: 对，我很高兴你提这个，因为人们已经太习惯那个快捷方式：你直接给我答案。首先，你助长了无力感。你绝对没帮他们学习和成长。如果你多少认为经理的工作至少是有时那么做——有时人会说“你不能就给我答案吗？”——而我总说：我能，但这就是我不那么做的原因，因为我觉得那不会服务你，因为那不是我的工作。我的工作不只是给你答案。我的工作是把你变成最终自己就知道正确答案的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But just give me the answer. Does this apply to friendships also? I know often people come to you as a friend, I need some advice on this. Does this apply as well? Often try not to give advice, or is it a different dynamic there?
turns.zh: 但就给我答案。这对友谊也适用吗？我知道常有人作为朋友来找你“我需要点建议”。也适用吗？常试着不给建议？还是那是不一样的动态？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Well, some of the same power differential can happen. I think chapter four in the book is about two guys who were good friends and one of them is always trying to give advice to the other one. First of all, it can be annoying if you didn't ask for it. So I certainly wouldn't give advice unless somebody asked for it, and I might not immediately jump to the advice, I might want to explore. What have you already thought about? How have you already approached it? Where are you stuck? I might ask more questions before I immediately go into advice because by the way, nine times out of 10, you end up giving advice on something that's not really what the person was worried about or wondering about. So first go to inquiry. You can always come back to advice.
turns.zh: 嗯，有些同样的权力差会发生。我觉得书里第四章讲两个好朋友，其中一个总想给另一个建议。首先，如果你没问，那会烦人。所以我当然不会给建议，除非有人问；而且我可能不会立刻跳到建议，我想先探索。你已经想过什么？你已经怎么处理了？你卡在哪？我可能在进建议前先问更多问题，因为顺便，十次有九次你最后给的建议，根本不是那人真正担心或在意的。所以先去询问。你随时可以回到建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I find that every time I try to resist or I make myself resist giving advice and instead ask more questions, every single time, I realized, okay, I had no idea what they were actually looking for or what was going on, but it's hard to do. I'm just like, here, I just want to tell you, here's the thing.
turns.zh: 我发现每次我试着忍住、逼自己不给建议、而是问更多问题，每一次我都意识到：好吧，我根本不知道他们真正在找什么、或在发生什么，但这很难做。我就是想：来，我就想告诉你，事情是这样的。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Totally. Because you know what? It's another mental model. I serve you best by just giving you advice when you ask for it, that's the loving, caring thing to do. Well, it's a mental model. Try testing it and seeing whether or not it really turns out to still be valid.
turns.zh: 完全。因为你知道？那是另一个心智模型。你一问我就给建议，那是对你最好的，那是充满爱、关心的事。嗯，那是心智模型。试着检验它，看它是否真的还成立。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so maybe the more correct mental model is how would you describe it that it's often better to help the person figure it out, or is it that you just often don't actually understand what's going on?
turns.zh: 所以也许更对的心智模型是：你怎么描述——常常更好地是帮人自己想出来，还是说你常常其实不理解在发生什么？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: The best thing to do first go to inquiry. Because by the way, I also, as you might imagine, I tend to err very much on the side of transparency, and so I'll say, man, I got all kinds of things going on in my head about what I think would be great for you to do, and I'm going to resist that because I, first of all may or may not hit the mark, so I'd really like to understand more. And second of all, I wonder if in the end be even more fruitful if we explore different things together.
turns.zh: 最好的事是先去询问。因为顺便，你也能想到，我极度偏向透明，所以我会说：老兄，我脑子里有一堆我觉得对你超好的事，而我要抵抗那个，因为首先我可能 hit 中、也可能没中，所以我真想多理解。其次，我想也许最后如果我们一起探索不同东西，会更有成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a few more questions. One is, so we have this segment on the podcast that I call Failure Corner, where people share failure in their career and what they learn from it, and you have a really constructive way of thinking about failure with this great acronym. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 还有几个问题。一个是，我们播客有个环节叫“失败角落”，人们分享职业里的失败和学到的。你对失败有个很建设性的思考方式，用一个超棒的缩写。能聊聊吗？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: The acronym is A-F-O-G, another F-ing... I don't know your audience well enough. Don't want to offend anybody.
turns.zh: 缩写是 A-F-O-G，another f-ing……我对你听众不够了解。不想冒犯任何人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go for it. If you feel like-
turns.zh: 说吧。如果你觉得——

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Another Fucking Opportunity for Growth. Every student who ever took a class from me, every client who I have ever coached, every participant who's ever gone through Leaders in Tech knows that acronym because my question, when something has gone wrong or a person has experienced a failure, my first question is always, so what did you learn? Because there's always a lesson, and then usually what follows is, yeah, you just had an AFOG. And as a person who's had a lot of AFOGs throughout my life, it puts it in perspective. I like the perspective that it offers, so it's not the end of the world. Sometimes AFOGs are more painful than others. Some AFOGs take longer to recover from than others. Most of the time they're recoverable, particularly if I've invested the energy in really unpacking what there was for me to be to learn.
turns.zh: Another Fucking Opportunity for Growth（又他妈一个成长机会）。每个上过我课的学生、每个我教练过的客户、每个走过 Leaders in Tech 的人，都知道这个缩写，因为当某事出错或某人经历失败时，我的第一个问题永远是：那你学到了什么？因为总有教训，然后通常跟着的是：对，你刚经历了一次 AFOG。作为一生有过很多 AFOG 的人，它让我有视角。我喜欢它提供的视角，所以那不是世界末日。有时 AFOG 比其他更痛。有些 AFOG 恢复得比别人久。大多数时候是可恢复的，尤其如果我为真正拆解“有什么是我该学的”投入了精力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. So the advice here is when something goes wrong, when you fail, think of it as another fucking opportunity for growth, AFOG.
turns.zh: 对。所以这里的建议是：当出错、当你失败，把它想成“又他妈一个成长机会”，AFOG。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 正是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: That's exactly right.
turns.zh: 完全对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To even go full circle to where we started building exceptional relationships, building robust relationships. In the book, you have this checklist of just how to build an exceptional relationship. I know you don't have all this in your head, whatever.
turns.zh: 回到我们起点——建立卓越关系、牢固关系。书里你有个“怎么建卓越关系”的清单。我知道你不一定全记在脑子里，whatever。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Actually I probably do.
turns.zh: 其实我大概记得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You probably do. What's on this list of just things you can do to build exceptional relationships?
turns.zh: 你大概记得。这清单上“你能做的建卓越关系的事”有什么？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Well, you can go back to the fact that there are six characteristics of exceptional relationships, and actually those are the characteristics that are present as a relationship is moving down this continuum that we've talked about. And the more each of these exists, the farther down the continuum you are. So the first one is I'm better known by you, and of course there's skills involved in how do I allow myself to be known. The second one is, I know you better and there's skills involved in getting to know you better. We've talked about many of them. The third one is we trust that our disclosures won't be used against us. The fourth one is we can be honest with each other. That's where all the feedback comes in. The fifth one is we know how to resolve conflict productively, and the sixth one is we are committed to each other's learning and growth. And when all six of those are present to varying degrees, you've moved farther down the continuum.
turns.zh: 嗯，你可以回到：卓越关系有六个特征，而事实上，那些特征就是一段关系沿着我们聊的连续体往下走时逐渐出现的。每一个存在得越多，你越往连续体下端走。所以第一个是：我被你更了解——当然，怎么允许自己被了解，涉及技能。第二个是：我更了解你——更了解你，涉及技能。我们聊过很多。第三个是：我们相信我们的披露不会被用来对付我们。第四个是：我们能对彼此诚实。所有反馈都从这里来。第五个是：我们知道怎么建设性地解决冲突。第六个是：我们承诺彼此的学习和成长。当这六个都以不同程度存在，你就沿连续体走得更快了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You wrote somewhere that you know your relationship has become exceptional when you and the other person don't have to hide important parts of yourself and can deal with major issues even if it feels scary.
turns.zh: 你在某处写过：当你和对方不必隐藏自己重要的部分、即便害怕也能处理重大问题，你就知道关系变卓越了。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Yep. I did write that somewhere and I stand by that.
turns.zh: 对。我确实在某处写过，我坚持这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you zoom out from all of your work and teachings, are there any overarching themes that continue to come up that you think are important for people to take away from this conversation?
turns.zh: 如果你从你所有工作和教学里 zoom out，有没有什么总出现的主题，是你觉得人们该从这次对话带走的？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Well, for starters, we're all works in progress, which means every relationship in your life is a work in progress. Because if I'm a work in progress and you're a work in progress, then by default so is our relationship. And so remembering that what worked with you two years ago may or may not work for you now because we're different people. So I think that's a biggie. I think stopping and becoming aware of what are the mental models that are driving these choices that I'm making, every behavior has in front of it a choice. If we stop long enough to become aware of it and in front of every choice, there's some belief. So I try to march myself back from the result to the behavior, to the choice, to the mental model that drove it or the skill or lack of skill.
turns.zh: 首先，我们都是半成品（进行时），这意味着你生命里每一段关系都是半成品。因为如果我是半成品、你是半成品，那默认我们的关系也是。所以记住：两年前对你管用的，现在可能管用、也可能不管用，因为我们是不同的人。所以我觉得那是大头。我觉得停下、觉察到“驱动我这些选择的心智模型是什么”很重要，每个行为前面都有个选择。如果我们停得够久、觉察到它，每个选择前面都有某个信念。所以我试着让自己从结果往回走：结果→行为→选择→驱动它的心智模型、或技能、或缺乏技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that we didn't talk about at the beginning of this because it might distract people, but you've been dealing with Long COVID for almost two years at this point. Where are you at with it? How are things going and is there anything you've learned from this unexpected part of your life?
turns.zh: 有件事我们开头没聊，因为可能分散人注意力，但你现在应对 Long COVID（长期新冠）快两年了。你目前状态如何？进展怎样？从这段意外的人生里学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: It's given me an opportunity to live a lot of what I teach. So I always taught in my leadership classes that the worst thing a leader can do is make an organization too dependent on them. If you care about building a sustainable long-term organization and a legacy, then it behooves you not to make the organization very dependent on you. So over the last 20 months, I have slowly and surely given more and more of my responsibilities to more and more members of the team to the point where hot off the press, I'm about to become only an advisor and step out of really all of my operational duties probably by the end of this year. Now, there was a point at which I was like, and oh my God, what happens if I get better suddenly? Because people do get better, and one of my very wise children said, "Mom, I'm pretty sure that if you suddenly get a lot better, they'll be happy to give you lots of stuff to do." So, anyway, that's one of probably the biggest lessons, and also it goes with a lesson around acceptance and accept. (01:23:25): I wrote a LinkedIn, I think a LinkedIn, not a blog paper, one of those LinkedIn things. If you go to my website, you can look at things I've written, I think it was called Long COVID and Acceptance or something like that. But it's about how acceptance is not resignation, and it's about having an opportunity to rethink a lot of things and reframe beliefs. And I think the last thing I'll say about it is that it has made me a much more empathetic person, and I think one of the really interesting and important things to learn and have always continued to learn in doing the interpersonal dynamics work we do is you never know what's going on for someone else. (01:24:26): And one of the worst things we can do is assume we know what's going on for someone else, and it's really easy to get really... I think I said this before we even got online, which is in the absence of data, people make shit up. So if you don't want people to make shit up about you, you're better off disclosing more because then you'll have more control over your self-definition, not less. People like to make sense of things. They will connect dots however way they want to unless you help them connect them the way you want them to. Another case for self-disclosure.
turns.zh: 它给了我机会，去活出我教的很多东西。所以我总在领导力课上教：领导者能做的最糟的事，是让组织太依赖自己。如果你在乎建一个可持续的长期组织和 legacy，那不该让组织太依赖你。所以在过去 20 个月，我缓慢但坚定地把越来越多责任交给越来越多团队成员，到最新进展，我快只当顾问了，大概今年底退出几乎所有运营职责。现在有过一个点，我想“天哪，如果我突然好了怎么办？”因为有人确实会好，我一个超聪明的孩子说：“妈，我相当确定如果你突然好很多，他们会很高兴给你很多事做。”所以，总之，那是大概最大的教训之一，它也连着一个关于接纳（acceptance）的教训。（01:23:25）我写了个 LinkedIn——我想是 LinkedIn，不是博客——那些 LinkedIn 东西之一。如果你去我网站，能看到我写的东西，我想叫“Long COVID 与接纳”或类似的。但它讲的是：接纳不是放弃，而是有机会重新想很多事、重构信念。我想说的最后一点是：它让我成了更有同理心的人，而我觉得在做我们这种人际动力学工作时，一直学到、也该一直学的最重要的事之一，是你永远不知道别人那边在发生什么。（01:24:26）我们能做的最糟的事之一，是假设自己知道别人那边在发生什么；在没数据的情况下，人很容易变得真的……我好像在线上之前就说过：在缺乏数据时，人们会编瞎话。所以如果你不想让人们编瞎话……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, Carole, I'm incredibly thankful that you made time for this. I know it's not the easiest thing to do these things.
turns.zh: 嗯，Carole，我特别感谢你抽时间做这个。我知道做这些不是最容易的事。

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To remind people where to find Leaders in Tech and how to apply, tell them the website and who it's for specifically, so the right people go there. And then finally, just how can listeners be useful to you as a final question?
turns.zh: 提醒人们去哪找 Leaders in Tech、怎么申请，告诉他们网站、特别是为谁准备的，好让对的人去。最后，作为最后一个问题，听众能怎么帮到你？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: I'm on LinkedIn. You won't be able to just connect with me. I've got one of those things where you can't just connect. You need my email address so you can put my email address in the notes. Anybody's more than welcome... But if you connect with me, please don't try to sell me anything. The only reason it's set up that way is that too many people were trying to sell me too many things and I got exasperated. That's the only reason they wanted to connect. So I'm just going to trust that you'll reach out to me because you want to connect with me because you're interested in my work and that you'll also know and be sensitive to the fact that I have Long COVID. So my capacity to respond to messages and emails is definitely impacted. I used to be one of those you could count on me to always respond. By the way, another learning. It turns out everybody didn't write me off just because I couldn't respond to them right away.
turns.zh: 我在 LinkedIn。你不能直接加我。我有那种“不能直接加”的设置。你需要我的邮箱地址，所以你可以把邮箱放备注里。任何人都非常欢迎……但如果你加我，请别试图卖我任何东西。它之所以那样设置，唯一原因是太多人想卖我太多东西，我烦了。他们想加的唯一理由就是卖东西。所以我只信任你会因为对我的工作感兴趣而联系我，也相信你知道、并敏感于我有 Long COVID。所以我能回消息和邮件的容量肯定受影响。我以前是那种“你指望我总会回”的人。顺便，另一个学习：结果大家并没有因为我不能立刻回就当我不存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really great learning. Okay. And then the website for people that may want to apply and the applications are still open basically by the time this is leadersintech.org?
turns.zh: 那是很好的学习。好。然后想申请的人去的网站，申请基本到这期上线时还开着，是 leadersintech.org？

turns.speaker: Carole Robin
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Amazing. Carole, you are wonderful. Thank you so much for making time for this. Thank you for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Carole，你太棒了。非常感谢抽时间。感谢你来。

turns.en: Thank you.
